forms.name: Claymation
forms.what: Figures of clay or plasticine, posed and photographed one frame at a time. Soft, lumpy, a little uneven, and never perfectly smooth in motion.
forms.origin: Plasticine dates from 1897. Art Clokey (Gumby) and Aardman, founded in 1972, made the look famous.
rules: Rounded volumes with small lumps and dents, never a perfect sphere
Matte, high-roughness surfaces under soft light
Saturated colour, few of them
Small asymmetries; a silhouette that changes slightly between poses
A miniature set: a floor, a backdrop, shallow depth
forms.timing: Shot on doubles: about 12 pose changes a second inside a 24 frames-a-second film. Each held pose sits a hair differently from the last.
build: Three.js: `MeshStandardMaterial` with roughness about 0.9, metalness 0, and a noise canvas as `bumpMap`
Push each vertex in or out by a few percent with a seeded hash, then `computeVertexNormals()`
Pose from stepped time: `held(t, 12)`
Add a seeded nudge per drawing to position and rotation (about 2% of the size)
A hemisphere light plus one soft key; no hard specular highlights
forms.assets: Geometry in code (spheres, capsules, lathes) for simple characters. Fingerprint or noise detail as a generated bump texture. A real character needs modelling.
forms.sound: Close foley on pose changes (soft thuds, squelches), light percussion. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth 24 or 30 frames-a-second motion: it reads as CG, not clay
Glossy plastic highlights
Perfect symmetry and clean edges
forms.blender: Use Blender when the clay needs real subsurface scattering, soft area-light shadows or sculpted detail.

forms.name: Stop-motion look
forms.what: Any real object moved and photographed a pose at a time. On screen it shows as stepped motion, tiny position errors and light that flickers a little.
forms.origin: As old as film: stop tricks appear in the 1890s. Pixilation, cut-out and puppet animation are all forms of it.
rules: Real materials: wood, card, cloth, plastic
Position jitter of a pixel or two between drawings
Lighting that varies slightly frame to frame
Hard cuts between poses, no in-between blur
forms.timing: On twos (12 changes a second) is the usual cadence; action sometimes on ones, held moments on threes or more.
build: Quantise time before anything else: `const ts = held(t, 12)`
GSAP: `ease: "steps(12)"` on a one-second tween does the same for a tween
Jitter and flicker keyed to the frame number: `jit(frameOf(t, 12), i, 1.2)`
Keep the camera and background steady: step the subject, not the world
forms.assets: None needed. Everything is procedural.
forms.sound: Foley that lands on pose changes. A bed that is not too smooth. Practice note.
pitfalls: Stepping the camera and background together, so everything strobes
Easing between held poses, which defeats the look
Jitter so large the object vibrates

forms.name: Paper cut-out
forms.what: Flat shapes cut from paper or card, layered, and moved a pose at a time. Parts hinge at joints; nothing bends.
forms.origin: Lotte Reiniger's The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926) is the oldest surviving animated feature. Terry Gilliam's Monty Python animations and the South Park pilot used cut paper.
rules: Flat fills with hard, slightly uneven cut edges
Layers stacked with a small, tight shadow under each
Rigid parts that rotate about a pivot
Paper grain over everything
A limited, slightly muted palette
forms.timing: Stop-motion cadence, usually on twos. Motion is rotation about joints and sliding, with pops and holds.
build: Each part is its own shape; nudge the corners with a seeded hash so edges look cut by hand
Canvas: `shadowOffsetY` 3 to 4 px with `shadowBlur` 4 to 5 px per layer. DOM: `filter: drop-shadow()`
Joints: rotate about a pivot (`transformOrigin` in GSAP, `translate` then `rotate` on a canvas)
Paper grain: a noise texture drawn once and laid over with `multiply`
SVG route: `feTurbulence` into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 2 to 4) roughens an edge
forms.assets: Shapes drawn in code or as SVG. Photo cut-outs need images you own, or generated ones.
forms.sound: Paper rustle, snips, soft ticks on pose changes. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth vector motion with no stepping
Perfect edges
Large soft shadows, which look like interface cards, not paper
forms.blender: Use Blender for real folded paper with thickness and light passing through it.

forms.name: Felt and fabric craft
forms.what: Shapes that look needle-felted or sewn: a fuzzy edge of loose fibres, a matte mottled surface, visible stitches.
forms.origin: Needle felting tangles wool fibres with barbed needles to make flat pictures and soft figures.
rules: A halo of short fibres along every edge
Matte, slightly mottled colour
Stitches: a dashed line just inside the edge
Chunky, simple forms in wool colours
forms.timing: Stop-motion cadence, on twos. Gentle bobbing and nudging.
build: Draw the shape, then several hundred short strokes outward from its edge, each angled by a seeded hash
Stitches: `setLineDash([9, 7])` on a path just inside the edge (SVG: `stroke-dasharray`)
Mottle: a grain texture clipped to the shape with `multiply`
SVG route: high-frequency `feTurbulence` (0.8 to 1.2) with displacement scale 3 to 6 on the edge
forms.assets: Procedural. A felt texture from an image model helps for close-ups.
forms.sound: Soft, warm, acoustic. Practice note.
pitfalls: Crisp vector edges
Flat plastic colour
No fibre fuzz
forms.blender: Use Blender hair or fur for real fibre fuzz on 3D figures.
forms.thin: The craft is well documented; its use in animation is a practice note, not sourced.

forms.name: Origami
forms.what: Paper folded from a flat sheet: sharp creases, flat facets, each fold a clean move followed by a pause.
forms.origin: Japanese paper folding. Modern computational origami works from crease patterns.
rules: Sharp mountain and valley creases
Flat facets, each shaded as one plane
Paper coloured on one side, white on the other
Soft, even light so the creases read
forms.timing: Folds are eased moves of about 0.8 seconds with a short hold after each. Smooth, not stepped.
build: 2D: a fold is a point travelling across the crease; draw the moving flap from the crease to that point
Shade the flap by its angle, and swap to the paper's other colour past 90 degrees
3D: flat-shaded polygons, child groups rotating about the crease axis
An orthographic camera gives a diagram-clean view
forms.assets: Geometry in code. A faint paper grain.
forms.sound: Light paper crinkle on each fold, soft piano or music box. Practice note.
pitfalls: Faces passing through each other
Folding with no hold, so the eye cannot follow
Light that hides the creases
forms.blender: Use Blender when the paper has to bend or show thickness.

forms.name: Shadow puppetry
forms.what: Flat figures held between a lamp and a cloth screen: dark silhouettes with punched patterns on a warm, glowing field.
forms.origin: An old tradition across Asia. Ravana Chhaya of Odisha uses uncoloured deerskin puppets with no joints; wayang kulit of Java and Bali was recognised by UNESCO in 2003. Lotte Reiniger brought silhouettes to film.
rules: Black silhouettes on a warm lit screen, never on white
Interior detail made of perforations: rows of holes and cut patterns
A lamp that flickers
The shadow softens and grows as the puppet moves away from the screen
Rods visible below the figures
forms.timing: Live puppets move continuously on rods; film versions are stop-motion, so use twos. Stiff, deliberate moves; no squash and stretch.
build: One path per puppet filled with the even-odd rule, so holes are part of the figure
Screen: a radial gradient from warm yellow to deep brown
Flicker: scale the lamp brightness by a seeded value per drawing
Distance from the screen: `filter: blur()` growing with distance, and lower opacity
Ravana Chhaya style: no joints, move and tilt the whole puppet. Wayang style: hinge the arms
forms.assets: Simple figures in code. Ornate traditional figures need drawing or tracing with care.
forms.sound: Narrator, singers and percussion in the tradition: cymbals and drums for Ravana Chhaya, gamelan for wayang.
pitfalls: Black on white, which loses the lamp
Smooth modern vector motion
Careless drawings of sacred figures: check the iconography with a source
forms.blender: Use Blender for real light through translucent coloured leather.

forms.name: Collage and mixed media
forms.what: Pieces of different papers, photographs and print stuck together: mismatched scale and texture, torn edges, hard shadows.
forms.origin: From the French coller, to glue. Braque and Picasso brought it into modern art around 1912; Dada followed with photomontage.
rules: Torn or cut edges
Mixed materials: flat colour, halftone photograph, tape
Overlap with a hard, offset shadow
Mismatched scale on purpose
One palette holding it together
forms.timing: On twos or threes. Pieces pop into place on the beat with a small rotation, then hold.
build: Torn edge: walk the outline of a rectangle and nudge every point with a seeded hash
Hard shadow: `shadowBlur: 0` with an offset of 5 to 6 px
Halftone a photo: dots on a staggered grid sized by brightness
Entrance: scale from 1.25 to 1 with a quarter-turn of rotation over a quarter of a second
forms.assets: Paper textures in code. Photo fragments need images you own, or generated ones.
forms.sound: Bright percussive music, staccato effects on each pop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Everything neatly aligned
No shadows
Too many unrelated colours and typefaces

forms.name: Risograph and halftone print
forms.what: The look of a cheap stencil print: two to four bright inks laid over each other, visible grain, dot screens, and layers that never quite line up.
forms.origin: The Risograph duplicator dates from 1980: one ink per drum, so each colour is a separate pass. Halftone dots go back to the 1860s.
rules: Two to four spot colours, often pink, blue and yellow
Inks overprint to make new colours (multiply)
Each layer sits a pixel or two off register
Grain and dot screens; no smooth gradients
Off-white paper
forms.timing: Print is still. Animate by re-rolling the misregistration and swapping the grain 8 to 12 times a second.
build: Each ink is its own layer drawn with `mix-blend-mode: multiply` (canvas: `globalCompositeOperation`)
Offset each layer by a seeded amount per drawing: `jit(frameOf(t, 8), layer, 3)`
Tone as dots: a staggered grid of circles whose radius follows the tone
Grain: several pre-made noise tiles, cycled by frame number
Three.js `HalftonePass` exists for 3D scenes; SVG `feColorMatrix` separates a photo into one ink
forms.assets: All procedural. A chunky sans or slab typeface.
forms.sound: Lo-fi, tape hiss. Practice note.
pitfalls: Gradients
Perfect registration
More than four colours

forms.name: Anime and cel shading
forms.what: Light broken into two or three flat tones with a hard edge between them, and an ink outline around every form.
forms.origin: Named after the celluloid sheets of hand-drawn animation. In 3D it became toon shading, as in Jet Set Radio and The Wind Waker.
rules: Two or three tone bands with hard edges
Shadows tinted with colour, not black
A clean outline
Flat, detailed backgrounds behind simpler characters
Limited animation: holds, then sudden moves
forms.timing: On twos as the baseline, ones for key action, threes and holds for dialogue.
build: Three.js `MeshToonMaterial` with a `gradientMap`: a three-texel `DataTexture` with `NearestFilter`, so light snaps to bands
Outline by inverted hull: a second copy of each mesh, slightly larger, drawn back faces only in black
`OutlineEffect` and `SobelOperatorShader` in the three.js examples are the two other routes
Step the pose time: `held(t, 12)`
2D: flat SVG shapes, a thick outline, `steps()` timing
forms.assets: The gradient map is three bytes. Characters need modelling or generated models.
forms.sound: Whoosh and impact effects on key poses. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth interpolation at 24 frames a second
More than three bands
Shadows that are only a darker grey
forms.blender: Use Blender for Freestyle line art and shader-to-RGB ramps on real characters.

forms.name: 2D flat vector explainer
forms.what: The plain explainer look: flat fills, a few colours, simple shapes and icons, smooth eased motion.
forms.origin: Flat design comes from Swiss style and modernism; in animation its ancestor is the stylised, limited look of the UPA studio.
rules: Flat fills, three to five colours, one accent
Geometric shapes with one stroke width
Plenty of space; one idea per frame
Clean sans type
forms.timing: Smooth ease-out moves of 0.4 to 0.8 seconds, staggered, with holds long enough to read.
build: HTML or SVG with GSAP: this is what HyperFrames is best at
Stagger related items 0.15 to 0.25 seconds apart
Draw check marks and connectors on with `stroke-dashoffset`
Move a highlight instead of cutting
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Soft interface blips, a light bed, voice-led pacing. Practice note.
pitfalls: A grid of identical cards
Gradients and shadows creeping in
Too much on screen at once

forms.name: Whiteboard and doodle
forms.what: Marker lines that draw themselves on a white board, in the order someone would draw them: simple diagrams and a few handwritten words, one accent colour.
forms.origin: Also called video scribing. A 2016 study found little evidence that it teaches better than other formats, so use it for its tone, not as a learning trick.
rules: Black marker lines with a slight wobble
Strokes appear in drawing order
One or two accent colours
A few handwritten words in one marker face, never paragraphs
forms.timing: Each element draws on over 0.3 to 1.5 seconds, paced to the narration. The line boils at about 10 changes a second.
build: Draw-on: a polyline drawn up to a fraction of its length (SVG: `stroke-dashoffset`)
Boil: nudge every point by a seeded amount keyed to `frameOf(t, 10)`
rough.js (MIT) generates sketchy shapes and hatching to animate afterwards
forms.assets: All in code. A marker or chalk typeface if the system has one.
forms.sound: Marker squeak, voice-led. Practice note.
pitfalls: Perfect vector lines
A hand that covers the drawing
Paragraphs of text

forms.name: Watercolour
forms.what: Transparent washes on textured paper: colour that spreads, pools darker at its edge, and lets the paper show through.
forms.origin: Pigment in water on paper. Wet-on-wet blends softly; wet-on-dry gives crisp edges.
rules: Transparent colour; overlaps make new colours
Darker pigment at the edge of each wash
Irregular, soft outlines
Paper grain visible everywhere
Unpainted paper as the highlight
forms.timing: Slow. A wash grows over 1 to 3 seconds with an ease-out. Hold drawings at 12 a second for a hand-painted feel.
build: Each wash: an irregular closed outline, clipped, filled with a radial gradient that is darkest near the rim
Layer washes with `multiply`
Paper grain over everything with `multiply`
SVG route: low-frequency `feTurbulence` (0.01 to 0.03) into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 10 to 25) for bleeding edges
3D: a Kuwahara filter as a custom pass gives a painterly result; three.js ships none
forms.assets: Procedural. A scanned paper texture improves close-ups.
forms.sound: Slow, gentle, acoustic. Practice note.
pitfalls: Opaque flat colour
A uniform blur, which looks out of focus, not painted
No paper texture
forms.thin: The edge-darkening rule is a practice note; the technique sources cover the filter, not the look.

forms.name: Ink wash (sumi-e)
forms.what: Black ink in every shade from deep black to pale grey, laid down in tapered brush strokes on rice paper, with a great deal left empty.
forms.origin: Chinese ink wash painting from the Tang dynasty, carried to Japan by Zen monks. Shanghai Animation Film Studio made ink-wash films from 1960.
rules: One ink, many dilutions
Strokes that taper from thick to a point
Empty paper as part of the picture
One small red seal
Soft grey washes behind sharp strokes
forms.timing: Slow and fluid. A stroke accelerates and lifts. On twos.
build: A stroke is a row of overlapping dots whose radius tapers along its length, drawn up to a fraction
Vary each dot's opacity with a seeded hash for a dry-brush break
Washes: soft radial gradients with `multiply`
SVG route: variable-width filled paths revealed by a mask
forms.assets: Procedural. Rice-paper grain.
forms.sound: Sparse: flute, single plucked notes, silence. Practice note.
pitfalls: Pure black on pure white
Uniform stroke width
Filling the frame

forms.name: Line art
forms.what: One weight of line on a plain ground, no shading: the drawing draws itself, then quivers slightly as if redrawn each frame.
forms.origin: Drawing with line alone, where tone comes only from hatching or stippling.
rules: A constant or tapered stroke with round ends
No fills, or one flat tone
Plenty of empty space
One accent colour at most
forms.timing: Draw-on over 1 to 2 seconds, then a boil at 8 to 12 changes a second.
build: Draw-on with `stroke-dashoffset` (canvas: a polyline to a fraction of its length)
Boil: a seeded nudge of 1 to 2 px per point, keyed to the frame number
SVG route: `feTurbulence` with `seed` set from the frame number, into `feDisplacementMap` (scale 1.5 to 3)
`vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke` keeps the weight when scaled
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A pencil or pen sound under the draw-on. Practice note.
pitfalls: Jitter so strong the line turns to noise
Filters that re-run on a large area every frame and slow the render

forms.name: Rotoscope look
forms.what: Real movement traced by hand: lifelike motion, flat colour fields that drift, and an outline that shimmers.
forms.origin: Max Fleischer built the rotoscope. A Scanner Darkly, Waking Life and the a-ha video for Take On Me are the well-known examples.
rules: Motion with the timing of live action
Flat or posterised colour fields
Outlines that change slightly every drawing
Colour that sits a little off the line
forms.timing: Every frame or on twos. The boil is keyed to the drawing.
build: From footage: draw each video frame to a canvas, posterise it, find edges (three.js has `SobelOperatorShader`), then nudge the edges per drawing
From code: a figure built from joints, drawn twice: thick flat colour offset by a seeded amount, then a thin outline with its own nudge
Re-encode source video with a keyframe on every frame so seeking is exact
forms.assets: Footage you own, or a figure built in code.
forms.sound: The original scene audio, or music-led. Practice note.
pitfalls: Edge noise that flickers out of control
Losing the subject in the treatment
Tracing footage you have no right to use
forms.blender: Dedicated tools do true painterly rotoscoping better than a browser.

forms.name: Motion comic
forms.what: Comic panels brought to life: layers inside a panel slide at different speeds under a slow camera move, then a hard cut to the next panel.
forms.origin: Watchmen: Motion Comic (2008) is the usual first example.
rules: Ink outlines, flat colour, halftone shading
A panel border
Foreground, figure and background on separate layers
Bursts and lettering as graphic elements
forms.timing: Slow pushes and pans of 2 to 4 seconds, hard cuts between panels, a pop for a burst.
build: Layers in a clipped panel; move far layers less than near ones
A slow scale from 1 to about 1.07 on the whole panel
Halftone shading: dots that shrink across the tone
Cut to the next panel by switching the scene at a time, not by cross-fading
forms.assets: Drawn panels in layers. Artwork needs an illustrator or generated images cut into layers.
forms.sound: Voice, music and effects carry it. Practice note.
pitfalls: A slow zoom on one flat image, which reads as a slideshow
No separation between figure and background
forms.thin: Pan-and-zoom staging is a practice note; the source describes the format, not the technique.

forms.name: UPA and mid-century modern
forms.what: Flat, stylised design from 1950s cartoons: geometric characters, abstract backgrounds, colour printed slightly off its outline, and very few drawings.
forms.origin: United Productions of America turned away from Disney realism and made limited animation a style. Gerald McBoing-Boing won an Academy Award in 1950.
rules: Characters built from triangles, circles and lines
Flat colour blocks that do not meet their outlines
Abstract backgrounds: a few shapes, no perspective
A warm, muted palette
forms.timing: Limited animation: a pose is held, then pops to the next. Eight or fewer changes a second.
build: Flat shapes; draw the outline 6 to 9 px away from the fill
Two or three poses, switched on a frame count with no in-betweens
Paper grain with `multiply`
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Jazz combo, sound effects as music. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth, fluid motion
Gradients and realistic light

forms.name: Rubber-hose cartoon
forms.what: The 1920s cartoon: limbs like hoses with no elbows or knees, round bodies that bounce to the music, black and white film.
forms.origin: Credited to Bill Nolan on Felix the Cat. The Fleischer studio kept it longest; Cuphead revived it.
rules: Curved tubular limbs
Round forms
Black and white or sepia, high contrast
Film grain, scratches and a frame that weaves slightly
Everything moves to the beat
forms.timing: Bouncy loops locked to the music, on twos, with squash and stretch.
build: A limb is a quadratic curve between two points; move the control point to bend it
Squash and stretch: scale the body on one axis by the inverse of the other
Grain: cycle a few noise tiles by frame; gate weave: shift the whole picture by a seeded pixel or two
Sepia with `feColorMatrix` if wanted
forms.assets: All in code. Original characters only.
forms.sound: Hot jazz, slide whistles, effects on every bounce. Practice note.
pitfalls: Stiff jointed limbs
Clean modern gradients
Copying characters that are still under copyright

forms.name: Linocut and woodcut print
forms.what: A relief print: bold flat shapes in one to three inks, with white gouge marks where the block was carved.
forms.origin: Carved in linoleum or wood; the uncut surface prints. Each colour is a separate block.
rules: Bold shapes, no fine detail
Short white cut marks inside the ink, all leaning one way
One to three inks, laid slightly off register
Paper showing at the edges
forms.timing: Each colour arrives as a pull, top to bottom, then holds. On twos or slower.
build: Draw each block to its own canvas, then cut marks out of it: short strokes with `destination-out`
Print blocks over each other with `multiply`, the second one offset a few pixels
Reveal a block by widening a clip from the top
SVG route: `feTurbulence` through a hard threshold makes rough voids
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A roller, a press, paper lifting. Practice note.
pitfalls: Gradients
Thin delicate lines
Too many colours
forms.thin: The source covers the technique; the visual rules are practice notes.

forms.name: Isometric
forms.what: A parallel projection seen from above at an angle: no perspective, three visible faces per block, a tidy model world.
forms.origin: A technical drawing projection. Games use a 2:1 pixel slope, about 26.6 degrees, which is strictly dimetric.
rules: No perspective: parallel lines stay parallel
Three tones per object: top lightest, one side mid, one side darkest
One light direction for everything
A grid floor
forms.timing: The camera does not orbit. Objects drop, stack and slide along the three axes, staggered by grid position.
build: 2D: `x = (gx - gy) * s`, `y = (gx + gy) * s / 2 - gz * s`; draw the two side faces, then the top
Sort by `gx + gy`, then by height, so nearer cubes cover farther ones
Three.js: an `OrthographicCamera` placed at equal x, y and z looking at the origin
CSS: `rotateX(60deg) rotateZ(-45deg)` on a flat layer
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Soft clicks as pieces land. Practice note.
pitfalls: A perspective camera by accident
Shadows that disagree with the light
Uneven block heights
forms.blender: Use Blender for bevelled, ambient-occluded isometric scenes.

forms.name: Low-poly 3D
forms.what: Meshes with few polygons, each face lit as one flat facet. A hardware limit that became a style.
forms.origin: From the era of early 3D consoles; chosen on purpose since about 2013.
rules: Visible facets, flat shaded
A limited, saturated palette
Simple lighting and a gradient or flat sky
Chunky silhouettes
forms.timing: Clean, so smooth: slow eased orbits and dollies at the full frame rate.
build: Low segment counts and `flatShading: true` on `MeshStandardMaterial`
Displace a plane's vertices with a seeded hash for terrain, then `computeVertexNormals()`
A hemisphere light plus one directional key; fog in the sky colour for depth
Camera position from `t` directly
forms.assets: Geometry in code for landscapes and props. Characters need modelling.
forms.sound: Calm, spacious. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth normals, which erase the facets
Detailed textures that fight the flat colour
forms.blender: Use Blender for modelling and baked light.

forms.name: Voxel
forms.what: Everything built from cubes of one size on a grid, like a three-dimensional pixel picture.
forms.origin: A voxel is a value on a 3D grid. Minecraft made the look familiar.
rules: One cube size, integer positions
Each face one flat tone
A small palette
Small floating scenes
forms.timing: On twos. Things appear cube by cube or layer by layer; moves snap to the grid.
build: One `InstancedMesh` of a box for all the cubes: one draw call
Set each cube's matrix from stepped time; hide a cube by scaling it to nothing
Cubes slightly under size (0.96) so the seams read
`MeshLambertMaterial` and a hemisphere light
forms.assets: Models as arrays in code, or made with a voxel editor.
forms.sound: Blocky, percussive, chiptune. Practice note.
pitfalls: Cubes at non-integer positions
Faces flickering where cubes touch at full size

forms.name: Pixel art
forms.what: A tiny picture placed pixel by pixel and scaled up with hard edges: a few colours, no blur, sprites that step.
forms.origin: From early video games; the term dates from 1982.
rules: A small canvas scaled by a whole number
A limited palette, often 8 to 32 colours
No anti-aliasing, no soft gradients
Sprites animate in a few frames
forms.timing: Walk cycles of 4 to 8 frames at about 8 a second. Scrolling moves in whole pixels.
build: Draw on a small canvas (160 by 90), then `drawImage` it up with `imageSmoothingEnabled = false`
CSS: `image-rendering: pixelated` on an upscaled canvas
Sprites as arrays of palette indexes
Three.js: `RenderPixelatedPass` renders a 3D scene to low resolution with nearest filtering
forms.assets: Sprites as data in code, or drawn in a pixel editor.
forms.sound: Chiptune. Practice note.
pitfalls: Scaling by a fraction
Mixed pixel sizes on one screen
Smooth vector edges or too many colours

forms.name: 3D product render
forms.what: A studio shot of an object: a seamless backdrop, soft key, fill and rim lights, controlled reflections, a slow turn.
forms.origin: Product photography lighting, done in 3D.
rules: A seamless backdrop
Key light to one side and above, a softer fill opposite, a rim light behind
A contact shadow under the object
True materials: gloss, metal, glass
One slow move
forms.timing: Smooth and slow at the full frame rate. The opposite of the handmade looks.
build: `MeshPhysicalMaterial` with `clearcoat` for lacquer, `metalness: 1` for metal
Three directional lights in the key, fill and rim positions, plus a hemisphere light
Contact shadow: a plane with a radial-gradient texture, `depthWrite: false`
Rotation from `t` directly; ease the camera, not the turntable
forms.assets: A model of the product: built in code, made with the 3D pack, or supplied.
forms.sound: Minimal: a low bed and one accent on the reveal. Practice note.
pitfalls: No reflections, so it looks like plastic
One harsh light
An object floating with no shadow
forms.blender: Use Blender when the brief asks for photoreal glass, caustics or depth of field.
forms.thin: The lighting source is about photography; applying it to rendering is a practice note.

forms.name: Kinetic typography
forms.what: Moving words as the whole picture: scale, weight and timing carry the meaning.
forms.origin: Saul Bass's title sequences for North by Northwest (1959) and Psycho (1960) made it a form.
rules: Type is the image; nothing competes with it
Strong contrast of size and weight
Words arrive in reading order, on the beat
One idea per frame
forms.timing: Each word lands in 0.3 to 0.5 seconds with a small overshoot, then the line holds long enough to read.
build: HyperFrames: split text into inline-block spans and stagger with GSAP
Canvas: `fillText` with a transform per word
Timing from the narration: one start time per word
Hold for (words / 3) + 0.5 seconds before the next line
forms.assets: A typeface with enough weights. No pictures.
forms.sound: Cut to the voice or the beat. Practice note.
pitfalls: Words faster than they can be read
Effects that add no meaning
Everything moving at once

forms.name: Infographic and data animation
forms.what: A chart that builds in a sensible order: axes, then the data from an honest baseline, then the exact values.
forms.origin: From Playfair's first charts in 1786 to animated infographics in music videos in 2002.
rules: One chart type that fits the data
Direct labels, not a legend
An honest axis: bars start at zero
One colour for the point being made
forms.timing: Axes in about half a second, each series over 0.8 to 1.5 seconds with an ease-out, then a hold to read.
build: Drive the chart from one time value; never use a chart library's own transitions
Bars grow from the baseline; counters show the rounded value as it grows and end on the exact figure
SVG or canvas with scale maths; D3 scales are enough
Every number needs a source in the brief
forms.assets: The data, with its source.
forms.sound: A tick or tone per value, a bed that stays out of the way. Practice note.
pitfalls: Numbers that were not checked
3D bars
An axis cut off to exaggerate a difference

forms.name: Lyric video
forms.what: The words of a song as the main image, each line timed to the vocal and the active word lit.
forms.origin: Lyric text appears in music videos from the 1980s; the format took off on video sites in the 2010s.
rules: Three to eight words on screen
The word being sung is brighter or larger
A background that never fights the text
One typographic system for the whole song
forms.timing: Locked to the music. A word changes exactly on its beat; a few frames late is visible.
build: Word start times from forced alignment or a beat grid
Compute the active line and word from `t`
A pulse from the beat phase: `1 - (beat % 1)` drives scale and background
Measure words first so the line is centred
forms.assets: The audio, with the right to use it, and its word timings.
forms.sound: The song.
pitfalls: Timing that drifts
Text over a busy background
Music you have no licence for

forms.name: VHS and glitch
forms.what: The damage of old tape and broken data: colour that bleeds sideways, scan lines, a band of noise at the bottom, sudden torn slices.
forms.origin: VHS records colour at far lower resolution than brightness, which is why colour smears. Glitch art uses such errors on purpose.
rules: Colour offset from brightness by a few pixels and softer
Scan lines
A tracking band of noise near the bottom
A date stamp in a blocky face
Glitch: slices displaced sideways, in short bursts
forms.timing: Full frame rate, with bursts of a fifth of a second. Seeds come from the frame number so every render matches.
build: Draw the clean frame to its own canvas first, then the damage on top
Redraw it in thin horizontal strips with a per-strip offset; large offsets only during a burst
Chroma bleed: a blurred copy drawn again a few pixels to the side with `screen`
Scan lines: a dark row every third pixel
Three.js: `FilmPass`, `RGBShiftShader` and `GlitchPass` exist; `GlitchPass` picks its own random timing, so check it repeats before relying on it
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Tape hiss, hum, a click on each burst. Practice note.
pitfalls: Constant glitching, which tires the eye
Glitching text the viewer has to read
Unseeded randomness, so two renders differ

forms.name: Blueprint and technical drawing
forms.what: White lines on blue: a grid, an object drawn in outline, centre lines, dimensions and a title block.
forms.origin: The blueprint is a cyanotype copy of an engineering drawing, introduced in 1842: white lines on blue.
rules: White or pale lines on a deep blue
A faint grid
Dashed centre lines, dimension lines with end ticks
A title block in a monospace face
forms.timing: Steady: lines draw on, then dimensions and labels fade in. No bounce.
build: Grid: thin lines every 30 px at low opacity (CSS: `repeating-linear-gradient`)
Draw-on with `stroke-dashoffset` or a partial polyline
Dashed centre lines with `setLineDash`
Dimension lines: a line, two end ticks and a centred label
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A pen plotter, a pencil. Practice note.
pitfalls: A neon blue
Labels that say nothing
Perspective in the drawing

forms.name: Neon sign
forms.what: Glass tubes bent into letters and lit: a bright core, a coloured glow, a dark wall, tubes that light one by one and sometimes flicker.
forms.origin: Glass tubing filled with gas and lit by electrodes; sections can be switched in sequence.
rules: One continuous line per letter, one width
A white-hot core inside a coloured halo
A dark wall behind
Letters light in sequence
forms.timing: Tubes come on in order with a short stutter each; now and then one dims for a frame.
build: Each tube is drawn three times: a wide faint stroke, a medium one, a thin white core, all with `shadowBlur`
Add them with the `lighter` blend (CSS: `mix-blend-mode: plus-lighter` or `screen`)
Flicker from `hash(frame, tube)`, never from a random call
Three.js: `UnrealBloomPass` for bloom on emissive geometry
forms.assets: Letter paths in code. A brick or plaster texture can be drawn.
forms.sound: A low electrical hum, a tick as each tube lights. Practice note.
pitfalls: A glow so wide the word cannot be read
Filled letters instead of a single tube
Flicker that differs between renders

forms.name: Pencil sketch
forms.what: Graphite lines on toothed paper: thin hatching that builds tone, a doubled and searching outline, and a thumb-smudged shadow. It looks drawn by hand because no two lines are quite the same.
forms.origin: Pencil marks are made by abrasion, a trail of graphite left on the paper. A large, very pure graphite deposit was found at Borrowdale in Cumbria, England, in 1565 (some sources say as early as 1500). Hatching, tone from closely spaced parallel lines, originated in the Middle Ages and developed into cross-hatching, notably in fifteenth-century prints.
rules: Thin grey lines with a slight wobble, and an outline drawn twice, a little differently each time
Tone comes only from line density: one set of hatching for light, a second set across it for shadow
A faint construction shape under the outline, as a sketcher would lay in first
A smudge where a thumb rubbed the shadow
Paper grain that breaks every line into specks
forms.timing: Lines appear in drawing order over about 3 seconds: construction line, outline, then each hatching layer, then the smudge. The picture steps about 8 times a second and each step re-seeds the wobble, like a stop-motion sketch.
build: Outline twice: two polylines with different seeded nudges of 1 to 2 px, keyed to `frameOf(t, 8)`, at different opacity
Hatching: parallel lines clipped to the shape with `ctx.clip(path)`; later layers use an even-odd clip so that they land only on the shadow side
Reveal each line from a fraction `k` of its length so the hatching sweeps on in order
Smudge: a radial gradient squashed to an ellipse and drawn with `multiply`
Tooth: specks in the paper colour drawn over the lines (`tooth()` in `looks-painted.js`)
forms.assets: All in code. A scanned sheet of cartridge paper makes a better ground if the user has one.
forms.sound: A pencil scratch under each hatching pass, quiet room tone. Practice note.
pitfalls: Hard black vector lines with no wobble
Perfectly even hatching that never re-seeds, which looks ruled by a machine
Shadow as a smooth gradient instead of lines

forms.name: Charcoal
forms.what: Soft black dust smeared and rubbed on rough paper: dark masses with crumbling edges, greys made by rubbing, and highlights lifted out with an eraser.
forms.origin: Charcoal was often a component of cave painting, with examples at least 28,000 years old. Artists use vine charcoal (wood burned in a kiln without air) or compressed charcoal held by a gum or wax binder; its marks are much less permanent than graphite, so lines are easily erased and blended.
rules: Soft, uneven dark masses; never a clean line or a hard outline
Edges crumble into specks and the paper grain shows through the black
Greys come from rubbing, not from a colour
Highlights are pale marks lifted out of the dark with an eraser: a sun, a glint on a trunk
One warm paper grey and black, nothing else
forms.timing: Marks are laid in order over about 3 seconds: broad rubbed sky first, then the dark mass, then the line work, then the lifted highlights. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Dabs: many overlapping low-opacity circles along a line, each with a seeded size and offset (`dabs()` in `looks-painted.js`); large dabs use a radial gradient so they stay soft
Rubbed sky: long, uneven strokes of varying width at low opacity
Eraser: paint pale strokes and a soft disc in the paper colour over the dark
Finish with coarse specks in the paper colour (`tooth()` with scale 2) and a dark vignette
forms.assets: All in code. A scan of grey sketching paper helps if the user has one.
forms.sound: Dry scratching and a soft smudging rub, room tone. Practice note.
pitfalls: Smooth airbrushed gradients with no grain
Crisp vector outlines on the tree or the figure
Pure black on pure white: charcoal lives on a warm grey ground

forms.name: Oil painting and impasto
forms.what: Thick oil paint laid in visible, directional brush strokes: colour mixed on the canvas, strokes that follow the shape of the thing, and raised light ridges where the paint is heaped up.
forms.origin: Oil painting binds pigment in a drying oil. The oldest known oil paintings are 7th-century Buddhist works in Afghanistan, and by the height of the Renaissance oil had almost replaced egg tempera for panel painting in most of Europe. Impasto is paint laid on thickly enough that brush or painting-knife strokes show.
rules: Visible brush strokes that follow the form: curved round a sun, straight along water
Each stroke has a light ridge on one side and a darker edge on the other, so the paint looks thick
Rich, mixed colour with small variations from stroke to stroke
Thick light daubs (impasto) on the brightest spots
A first blocked-in wash under the strokes
forms.timing: A first wash blocks the colour in, then strokes cover the canvas over about 3 seconds, the brightest daubs last. The picture steps about 12 times a second, like a timelapse of a painter.
build: Draw each stroke as a short thick line with round caps, three times: a dark copy offset down and right, the colour, and a thin lighter copy offset up and left (`brush()` in `looks-painted.js`)
Choose each stroke's angle from a flow field: tangent to circles round a focus, level over water
Choose colour from position with a seeded jitter per stroke so no two match
Reveal each stroke from a seeded start time so the canvas fills at random places
forms.assets: All in code. Three.js can use a normal map from the stroke ridges for a real impasto light, but the 2D version reads well.
forms.sound: Brush on canvas, a slow room tone, a calm piano or strings bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Strokes all the same angle, which reads as a filter
Smooth gradients inside the strokes
No ridge highlights, which makes the paint look flat and digital

forms.name: Gouache storybook
forms.what: Flat, matte, opaque layers of paint with hand-cut edges and faint brush streaks: the look of a printed picture book. Each colour is laid over the last, with no gradients and no transparency.
forms.origin: Gouache is an opaque water-medium paint of pigment, water and a binder such as gum arabic, with a high ratio of pigment to binder. It has been used for at least twelve centuries, dries to a matte finish, and is used by commercial artists for posters, illustrations and comics.
rules: Flat, fully opaque shapes in a small palette
Matte finish: no gloss and no shading gradients
Hand-cut edges, slightly uneven, never a perfect curve
Faint horizontal brush streaks inside each shape
Back to front: sky, far hills, near hills, then the subject, then small bright details
forms.timing: Layers go on one after another, each over about half a second: back to front over about 3 seconds, with small things such as stars and smoke last. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: One filled path per colour, built with `cut()` (corners nudged by a seed) or `blob()`
Clip to the path and draw 20 to 30 faint light and dark streaks across it (`flatShape()` in `looks-painted.js`)
Reveal each layer with a clip that grows: up from the bottom for ground, across for objects
Add paper tooth last at low strength
Glow from a window is two or three flat circles of falling opacity, not a gradient
forms.assets: All in code. Real gouache scans make a stronger texture if the user owns them.
forms.sound: Soft acoustic guitar or a music box, a wooden or paper foley on each layer. A storybook narration suits it. Practice note.
pitfalls: Gradients or soft shadows, which turn it into a digital illustration
Black outlines round every shape: gouache is edge to edge colour
Too many colours: a storybook palette is five or six

forms.name: Crayon and oil pastel
forms.what: Waxy, broken strokes of bright colour on toothed paper, scribbled in one slanted direction with fat outlines pushed past the edges. It looks like a child's drawing with real pressure in it.
forms.origin: A crayon is a stick of pigmented wax, in the modern English-speaking world mostly paraffin. In 1924 two Japanese teachers set out to make a high-viscosity crayon, the oil pastel, which binds pigment in wax and non-drying oil, so that children could draw freely in colour.
rules: Scribbled fills in one slanted direction, each pass with its own pressure
Paper tooth shows through the wax as speckles of paper colour
Fat outlines in a darker shade of the fill, pushed a little past the edge
Bright, simple, saturated colour: red roof, blue door, green grass
Simple subjects drawn the way a child would: sun with rays, house, tree
forms.timing: Each area is scribbled in over 0.3 to 0.9 seconds, sky and grass first, the subject after, small details last, about 4 seconds in all. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Scribble: near-parallel passes inside a rotated box, each stroke its own opacity and width (`scribble()` in `looks-painted.js`), clipped to the shape
A second, lighter, dashed pass at another angle across the first
Outlines: a fat, darker stroke with a seeded wobble that is re-seeded on each step
Tooth: coarse specks in the paper colour drawn over everything (`tooth()` with scale 2)
forms.assets: All in code. A scan of cream sugar paper helps if the user has one.
forms.sound: A waxy scratching sound under each scribble, a ukulele or xylophone bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Clean flat fills with no stroke direction
Thin precise outlines
Tooth specks so fine that they read as film noise

forms.name: Chalkboard
forms.what: White and coloured chalk on a dark green-black board: dusty, broken lines that draw themselves, ghosts of old eraser swipes, and a stub of chalk at the tip of each line.
forms.origin: A blackboard or chalkboard is a reusable surface written on with chalk (calcium sulphate or calcium carbonate). Early boards were slate; later ones are often dark matte paint, black or dark green. The first attested use of chalk on a blackboard in the United States dates to 21 September 1801.
rules: Dark green-black board with a soft lit patch and faint eraser swipes
Dusty, broken chalk lines: three thin passes and a soft halo, never a solid line
One or two chalk colours besides white
A wooden ledge with fallen dust under the board
Hand-lettered words, few and large
forms.timing: Each line draws on over 0.3 to 0.8 seconds, in the order a teacher would draw it, about 4 seconds in all. The line boils at about 10 changes a second.
build: Chalk: three passes of the same stroke with different dash patterns at half opacity plus a wide faint halo, each nudged by a seeded amount keyed to `frameOf(t, 10)` (`chalk()` in `looks-painted.js`)
A rounded stub drawn at the tip while the line is still drawing
Board: base colour, a radial light, grain, and a few big translucent ellipses for old swipes
Specks in the board colour drawn over the chalk eat holes in it
forms.assets: All in code. A chalk typeface if the system has one; the demo falls back to a handwriting face.
forms.sound: Chalk squeak and tap under each line, voice-led. Practice note.
pitfalls: A pure black board and perfect white vector lines
A hand that covers the drawing
Paragraphs of text

forms.name: One continuous line
forms.what: A whole subject drawn by one unbroken line on a flat colour: the pen never lifts, crosses itself where it must, and the finished drawing is a single curve.
forms.origin: In a continuous-line drawing the artist looks at both the subject and the paper, moving the medium over the paper to create a silhouette of the object. It belongs to the contour-drawing family, and line art in general is made of distinct lines placed against a plain background.
rules: One line, constant width, round ends, that never breaks
A flat single-colour ground and a single ink colour
The line crosses itself and doubles back rather than lifting
A pen dot at the tip while it draws
Plenty of empty space round the subject
forms.timing: The line draws on at an even speed over about 3.5 seconds, eased at the start and the end, then the drawing holds. Full frame rate: a clean ink line should not step.
build: Build the path as a smooth spline through hand-placed points (`spline()` in `looks-painted.js`)
Resample it to points evenly spaced by length, so the pen moves at a steady speed
Draw it to a fraction `k` of its length with `strokePart()`; round caps and joins
Put a filled dot at the point where the line currently ends
SVG route: `stroke-dashoffset` on a single path
forms.assets: All in code. Place the control points on a sketch of the subject first.
forms.sound: A pen on paper under the draw-on, then silence. A single sustained note or a gentle piano. Practice note.
pitfalls: Lifting the pen: a second path makes it a normal line drawing
Jitter or boil, which fights the idea of one smooth line
Too much detail: the form must read from the outline alone

forms.name: Paint-on-glass
forms.what: Oil paint smeared on a lit sheet of glass: translucent colour that glows against the light, deeper where it is thick, finger streaks dragged behind, and shapes that melt from one thing into the next.
forms.origin: A technique for animated films made by manipulating slow-drying oil paints on sheets of glass; gouache mixed with glycerine is sometimes used instead. The best-known practitioner is the Russian animator Aleksandr Petrov, who has used it in seven films, all of which have won awards.
rules: Translucent colour over a bright backlight: paint multiplies, so overlaps go darker
A thicker, darker rim round each daub
Finger streaks trailing behind moving shapes
Lines scratched through the paint that let the light through
One shape morphs into another instead of cutting
forms.timing: One frame at a time, about 12 changes a second. The picture is smeared and re-pushed on each step, so streaks and edges move a little every frame.
build: Draw the lamp as a radial gradient, then paint everything with `globalCompositeOperation = 'multiply'`
Each daub: a filled shape, a darker rim stroke, and a dozen gradient-faded streaks (`daub()` in `looks-painted.js`), with streak lengths re-seeded on each step
Morph by interpolating the shape parameters (size, angle, colour) with `easeInOut`
Scratches: switch to `source-over` and draw thin cream lines clipped to the shape
forms.assets: All in code. Real glass-paint scans work as a texture layer over the lamp.
forms.sound: A wet, squelching foley on every move, a slow and dreamy bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Opaque colour, which loses the glow
Sharp vector outlines round the shapes
Cuts between forms: the look depends on continuous morphing

forms.name: Sand animation
forms.what: A light table seen from above: a warm glowing backlight, sand as dark sepia masses, and light showing through wherever the sand is thin, with soft graded edges. The picture is made of filled shapes, and one shape is pushed into the next.
forms.origin: A form of stop motion in which sand is shaped under a camera, often lit from behind by a lightbox so that the thickness of the sand gives shading and lines. Sand art is older than film: Navajo, Aboriginal Australian and Tibetan cultures made it, and the Japanese bonseki has been practised since at least the 7th century. Swiss animators Gisèle and Nag Ansorge and the American Caroline Leaf took it up for films in the 1960s.
rules: A bright, warm backlight, strongest at the centre and falling off at the edges
Sand is dark sepia to near-black where it is thick; bright where there is no sand; amber and soft where it is thin
Filled masses with soft, graded edges, never outlines
One form flows into the next as a hand sweeps the sand: sun to flower to bird
Loose grains: dark specks on the light, bright pinholes in the dark masses
forms.timing: A figure grows in over about a second, then each change of form takes about 1.3 seconds. The picture steps about 12 times a second.
build: Paint the table as a radial gradient from pale cream to amber to brown

Describe each figure as the same number of soft ellipses (position, size, angle); blend two figures number by number with `easeInOut` to morph (`SAND_SUN`, `SAND_FLOWER`, `SAND_BIRD` in `looks-painted.js`)
Draw each mass three times with `filter: blur()`: a wide amber halo, a mid brown body, a dark core (`sandMass()`)
Heap a few dark grains at the edge while a shape is moving
Finish with dark and light speckle and a multiplied vignette
forms.assets: All in code. Real sand photographed on a light table makes a good grain layer.
forms.sound: A soft, dry, whispering rub as the sand moves, a slow music bed that suits a story. Practice note.
pitfalls: Bright outlines drawn on a dark ground: that reads as lines scratched in beach sand, not as sand on a light table
A flat brown background with no backlight glow
Hard-edged vector shapes: the edges of sand are soft and graded

forms.name: Madhubani (Mithila)
forms.what: Double black outlines round bright flat fills, with every gap packed with hatching, dots or small motifs: fish, peacocks and lotuses inside a decorated border, with no empty space. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: Madhubani art, also called Mithila art, is a style of painting practised in the Mithila region of Nepal and Bihar. It was traditionally created by women of various communities on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of huts, and is now also done on cloth, handmade paper and canvas, with natural dyes and pigments.
rules: Double black outlines: a bold line with a thin one inside it
Bright, flat colour: red, yellow, green and indigo, with black line work
Every gap is filled with hatching, dots, flowers, leaves or geometric marks: no empty space
Motifs from nature: fish, peacocks, lotus, the sun and moon, plants
A decorated border of triangles and flowers, drawn as part of the painting
forms.timing: Elements are drawn on in order over about 4 seconds: border, ground motifs, then the large figures. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Build each figure as a smooth closed spline (`closed()` in `looks-folk.js`) and draw it with `folkShape()`: the outline draws round, the fill comes in, a pattern fills it, then an inner line follows
Patterns clipped to the shape: parallel lines, dot grids and scale arcs (`lines()`, `dots()`, `scales()`)
Fill the ground first with a grid of small motifs, each chosen by a hash of its cell, so the gaps are never blank
Draw the border as a loop of triangles with a flower in each corner
forms.assets: All in code. Real work is done on handmade paper or cloth: a scanned paper texture helps if the user has one.
forms.sound: Soft folk percussion or a flute drone, a gentle brush sound as each figure draws on. Practice note.
pitfalls: Empty space: the form is defined by filling it
Single thin outlines and gradients
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Madhubani art
forms.thin: Wikipedia marks its line that no space is left empty, with the gaps filled by flowers, animals, birds and geometric designs, as needing a citation; confirm it against a museum or scholarly source before quoting it.

forms.name: Warli
forms.what: White figures drawn in simple shapes on a terracotta wall: a circle for a head, two triangles joined at their tips for a body, stick arms and legs, a ring of people dancing hand in hand round a tarpa player, trees, huts and a sun. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: Warli painting is tribal art made mostly by the Warli people of the North Sahyadri Range in Maharashtra, India, usually on the mud walls of village huts, in a white pigment of rice flour and water with a gum binder. Its basic shapes are the circle, triangle and square; people and animals are drawn as two inverse triangles joined at their tips, and the tarpa dance, in which men and women entwine hands and circle the tarpa player, is a central subject.
rules: White (rice-paste) lines and fills only, on a red-brown mud ground
Figures of a circle head and two triangles that meet at their tips, with stick limbs
A ring or spiral dance, hands joined, round a central player
Trees as a trunk with paired branches; a sun as a circle with strokes
Borders of repeating diamonds; huts as a square with a triangle roof
forms.timing: Figures appear one at a time over about 3 seconds and the spiral turns slowly while they step between two poses. The picture steps about 8 times a second, and the poses at 4.
build: Ground: base colour plus a dozen big soft radial gradients for daubed mud, then a fine speckle
A figure is two filled triangles, a disc and stroked limbs (`warliFigure()` in `looks-folk.js`), turned so the head points outward
Place figures along a spiral and add a slow rotation of the whole spiral from stepped time
Trees: a trunk and branches as paired strokes that shorten toward the top, a dot at each tip
forms.assets: All in code. A scan of a mud-plastered wall makes a stronger ground if the user has one.
forms.sound: Drum and tarpa-like reed drone, claps on the pose changes. Practice note.
pitfalls: Colour: the tradition is white on brown or red-brown
Rounded, realistic bodies
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Warli art

forms.name: Pattachitra
forms.what: Bold black outlines and flat colour on a prepared ground: a thick ornamental border, an almond eye in profile, scale and fin patterns, and flowers and tendrils packed round the subject. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: Patachitra or Pattachitra is a traditional cloth-based scroll painting of the eastern Indian states of Odisha and West Bengal; the name comes from the Sanskrit patta, cloth, and chitra, picture. The Odisha tradition originated at Puri, is painted in natural colours on cloth coated with chalk and gum, and has bold, clean lines with no landscape or perspective.
rules: A thick, ornamental border in red, yellow and black, with dots and zigzags
Bold, clean outlines and flat colour
Eyes in profile, drawn as an almond with a dark pupil
Dense floral fill: rosettes, leaves and spiral tendrils
Patterns inside the shapes: scales, fan lines, bands
forms.timing: The ground motifs fill in over about 3 seconds, the main figure draws on over about 1.5 seconds. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Draw the border as flat bands with dots and zigzags (`strokeRect`, dot loops)
Fill the ground with rosettes (`rosette()`) and spiral tendrils (`curl()`) on an offset grid
The figure is a closed spline drawn with `folkShape()`, a heavy 8 px outline and a scale pattern
An almond eye: a closed four-point spline with a dark disc inside
forms.assets: All in code. A scan of cloth or tea-stained paper helps if the user has one.
forms.sound: Drone and temple-bell texture, a rhythmic percussion under the border. Practice note.
pitfalls: Thin outlines, gradients and perspective: the tradition is flat
Drawing deity faces from memory: the demo uses a fish for that reason
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Pattachitra
forms.thin: The fish in the demo is a decorative study of the border, outline, eye and fill rules; the tradition itself mostly depicts Hindu deities and stories, which Wikipedia describes.

forms.name: Gond
forms.what: Animals and trees drawn in thin black outline and filled with bands of dots and dashes in bright colours, each band following the shape, on a light ground. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: The Gond, or Gondi, people are an ethnolinguistic group spread across central and eastern India, including Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh. The artist Jangarh Singh Shyam, born into a Pardhan Gond family in Patangarh, Mandla district, Madhya Pradesh, is credited with starting the school called Jangarh Kalam; he used lines of coloured dots, inspired by Gond tattoos, with bands of dots, dense cross-hatching and comb-lines, and painted animals such as tigers and deer.
rules: Thin black outlines round animals, birds and trees
Inside every shape: rows of dots, dashes, and dots and dashes, each row in its own bright colour
The rows follow the long axis of the shape
A light or bright ground, often with a dotted ground and border
Animals and trees shown as decorated cut-outs, with no shading
forms.timing: Parts draw on one after another over about 3 seconds, outline first, then the bands fill. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Draw each part with `folkShape()` and a pale tint fill
Bands: rows along the shape's axis with a gentle wave, alternating dots, ticks and dot-and-tick, cycling six colours (`gondBands()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Add a dot grid over the ground and a dotted border
Keep the outline thin so the dots and dashes carry the colour
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Drums and a stringed drone, a rhythmic tapping as each band fills. Practice note.
pitfalls: Solid fills and gradients: the pattern is the colour
Dots all the same size and colour
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Gond art
forms.thin: Wikipedia has no standalone Gond painting article, so the sources are the Gond people article and the article on Jangarh Singh Shyam, the artist most closely tied to the modern style. Confirm the wider tradition against a museum source before making claims in a film.

forms.name: Indian miniature (Mughal and Rajput)
forms.what: A small, richly detailed court painting in jewel tones: a flat, stacked space with no deep perspective, a gold border with a floral margin, fine ornament on every surface, and figures in profile. It is a living tradition with working artists; the demo here is a code study of its visual rules, not the craft itself, and a film should credit the tradition and, where it can, commission or license work from the artists.
forms.origin: Mughal painting is a style of miniature painting, used for book illustrations and album pages, that developed at the Mughal court between the 16th and 19th centuries; its portraits are normally in profile. Rajput painting is the painting of the regional Hindu courts during the Mughal era, from about the end of the 16th to the middle of the 19th century, and its conservative idioms keep bright colour, flatness and abstract form.
rules: Flat, stacked space: sky, palace, terrace and garden as bands, no deep perspective
Jewel tones: ruby, emerald, lapis, saffron and gold
A gold border with a floral margin, drawn as part of the painting
Figures in profile, small and seated, with turbans and robes
Fine ornament: domes, arches, flower beds, water channels
forms.timing: The border, the sky and the palace draw in over about 2 seconds, then the garden, water and figures. Birds drift and the fountain rises. The picture steps about 8 times a second.
build: Paint bands from back to front, each a flat fill with a thin dark line
Border: a ruby frame between gold lines with a row of small flowers (`rosette()`)
Domes: half-ellipses with ribs, a finial and a small disc
Figures: a robe polygon, a profile head with a nose notch, a turban ellipse and one arm to a cup
Animate only small things: birds, the fountain, the cloud ribbons
forms.assets: All in code. For real pages use public-domain scans from museum collections and say so in REPORT.md.
forms.sound: Sitar or santoor, a quiet fountain, birdsong. Practice note.
pitfalls: Deep one-point perspective and cast shadows
Photorealistic faces
Presenting a machine-made picture as authentic Mughal or Rajput work

forms.name: Engraving and banknote hatching
forms.what: Fine lines cut like a burin: hatching that follows the form and swells in the shadow, cross-hatching where it is darkest, a vignette of waves, and a woven guilloche frame, in one or two inks on cream paper.
forms.origin: Engraving is the practice of incising a design on a hard surface with a burin; the grooves can make an intaglio plate for printing. In traditional engraving, which is a purely linear medium, half-tones are made by many thin parallel lines, hatching, and two crossing sets of them are cross-hatching. Guilloché is a precise, repetitive pattern engraved by engine turning, and modern banknotes are almost always engraved.
rules: Tone from line only: thin lines in the light, thick lines in the shadow
Lines follow the form: curved round a sphere, not straight across it
Cross-hatching only in the deepest shade
A guilloche frame of interwoven waves and rosettes
One or two inks: a dark brown-black and a burgundy on cream paper
forms.timing: Lines are cut one after another from top to bottom over about 3 seconds, then the cross-hatching and frame. Full frame rate: an engraved line should not step.
build: Sphere: sample points with latitude, longitude and a tilt, and a brightness from a light direction (`spherePoint()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Stroke each short segment with a width of about `0.35 + 3.3 * (1 - brightness) ** 1.7`
Cross-hatch: a second family of lines drawn only where brightness is under 0.4
Guilloche: six sine waves in different phases across each side, and a rose curve at each corner
Background vignette: horizontal wavy lines whose width grows toward the edge, clipped to an ellipse
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A fine scratch under the line work, a quiet low tone. Practice note.
pitfalls: Lines of one width: the swelling is the engraving
Smooth gradients
Straight hatching that ignores the form

forms.name: Silkscreen poster
forms.what: A poster printed in a few flat inks that overprint, each a little out of register, with coarse halftone dots for tone: flat shapes, big blocks, and colours that mix where they overlap.
forms.origin: Screen printing, also silkscreening or serigraphy, transfers ink through a mesh onto a surface except where a stencil blocks it; traditionally the mesh was silk. It is widely used for posters and other graphics.
rules: Two to four flat inks, never more
Inks overprint with multiply, so overlaps make new colours
Each ink is a little off register, differently on each drawing
Halftone dots at an angle for gradients and glows
Bold flat shapes and block bars where type would go
Paper grain showing through
forms.timing: Each ink prints in turn, sliding into register over about 0.7 seconds, one every second. The picture steps about 8 times a second and each step re-seeds the misregistration.
build: One draw function per ink, drawn with `globalCompositeOperation = 'multiply'` (`inkLayer()` in `looks-folk.js`)
Offset each layer by a few pixels plus a seeded jitter keyed to `frameOf(t, 8)`
Halftone: a rotated grid of dots whose radius is `pitch * 0.72 * sqrt(value)` (`halftone()`)
Slide each layer in from off-register and settle it at its offset
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A press clunk and a squeegee sweep as each ink lands, an upbeat drum loop. Practice note.
pitfalls: Perfect register and soft gradients: that reads as digital
Too many colours
Transparency that does not multiply

forms.name: Art deco
forms.what: Gold lines, sunbursts and stepped, symmetric geometry on a deep ground: fans and arcs, a tower in steps, zigzag borders and small stars, in gold on navy and burgundy.
forms.origin: Art Deco first appeared in Paris in the 1910s, just before the First World War, and flourished internationally in the 1920s and early 1930s; the name came into use after the 1925 Paris exhibition of decorative and industrial arts. It has its origin in the bold geometric forms of the Vienna Secession and Cubism, and in New York the Empire State and Chrysler Buildings are monuments to the style.
rules: Strict symmetry about a vertical axis
Gold or light-gold lines on a deep ground: black, navy, burgundy or emerald
Sunburst rays, fans and concentric arcs
Stepped shapes: towers and frames in steps
Zigzag borders, chevrons and small star sparkles
forms.timing: Rays and arcs grow out from the centre over about 3 seconds, then the tower rises in steps. Smooth, full frame rate, with a slow twinkle.
build: Sunburst: wedges that alternate fill and ground, each edge a gold line drawn to a growing radius
Arcs: `ctx.arc` from pi to a growing angle at several radii
Tower: nested rectangles of falling width, each rising in turn
Mirror the side decoration with `ctx.scale(-1, 1)` so it is exactly symmetric
Sparkles: eight-point stars whose size follows a sine of time
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: Brass and muted trumpet, a swing bed. Practice note.
pitfalls: Asymmetry
Soft gradients and rounded shapes
Using teal or mint: this skill leaves them out

forms.name: Stained glass
forms.what: Coloured panes held by thick dark lead lines in an arched window: a rose at the top, a diamond lattice below, and light glowing through each pane.
forms.origin: Stained glass is glass coloured by adding metallic salts during its manufacture, arranged into windows of small pieces held together, traditionally, by strips of lead called cames. In Western Europe, together with illuminated manuscripts, such windows are a major form of medieval visual art that has survived.
rules: Thick, dark, even lead lines round every pane
Saturated, jewel-coloured panes: ruby, cobalt, emerald, amber, violet
Each pane glows brighter at its centre, as light passes through
A pointed or round arch, with a rose and a lattice
A dark stone wall round it, so the glass is the light source
forms.timing: The panes light up from the centre outward over about 2 seconds, then a soft beam of sun crosses the glass slowly. Smooth, full frame rate.
build: Build each pane as a polygon; fill dark, then fill with its colour as it is lit, plus a radial glow with `lighter`
Rose: annular sectors in three rings (`ring()` in the demo); lattice: a grid of diamonds clipped to the arch
Stroke every pane with a 6 px dark line, `lineJoin = 'round'`
The beam: a linear gradient band drawn with `lighter`, its position a function of time
Wall: dark base colour and a block pattern
forms.assets: All in code.
forms.sound: A choir pad, a long reverb, footsteps in a stone room. Practice note.
pitfalls: Thin lead lines: they are part of the picture
Flat panes with no glow
Washed-out pastel colours: keep them saturated
